strengths: The paper presents a clear and potentially useful problem formulation: explaining black-box behavior using human-interpretable, macro-level features rather than pixels, with an identifiable audience spanning causal discovery and XAI. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-xdl4g2l5/call-dc42f84ca1824dea85637a8901ac5855/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Using PAGs and FCI is conceptually appropriate when latent confounding is allowed. The paper explains the principal assumptions and edge types accessibly, and the synthetic example conveys why association alone can misidentify explanatory features.
The experiments span synthetic, natural-image, and medical-image settings, and the inclusion of bootstrapping and a GRaSP-FCI sensitivity analysis is valuable.
The manuscript is generally well organized and readable, with helpful graphical examples, preprocessing details, and a candid discussion of feature annotation and measurement error.
weaknesses: Necessary—The real-data studies do not validate the central causal claim. With neither known causal structure nor interventions on image concepts, clinical or ornithological plausibility only shows that the results are intuitive; it does not establish that the identified attributes causally affect the classifiers. The conclusions should be narrowed to exploratory candidate relations or supported with interventional/ground-truth validation.

Necessary—The X-ray design has severe selection and overlap problems: all controls are selected from images labeled “no findings,” while cases have pneumonia. Consequently, the seven finding indicators are structurally tied to case selection, and there is little or no support for contrasting findings among comparable pneumonia-negative images. This conflicts with the manuscript's dismissal of selection bias and makes causal interpretation of the learned PAG untenable without a redesigned cohort or an explicit selection model.

Necessary—The reported “edge stability” conflates directed edges with circle-to-arrow edges. A Zi circle-to-arrow Y edge remains compatible with pure latent confounding, especially because the arrowhead at Y is encouraged by the imposed background knowledge. Its bootstrap frequency is therefore neither calibrated causal confidence nor causal importance. Moreover, non-adjacency to Y does not exclude an indirect causal path. Claims that high-ranked variables are “likely causes” and low-ranked variables are causally irrelevant must be revised or analyzed using definite/possible ancestral relations separately.

Necessary—Finite-sample reliability is not established. Chi-square conditional-independence tests with 26 multi-category bird attributes, conditioning sets as large as four, and only 3,538 observations can create extremely sparse contingency tables; the X-ray analysis has only 240 observations. Bootstrap frequencies do not repair invalid or low-powered tests, and no calibration, null experiment, confidence assessment, or sensitivity to alpha and conditioning-set limits is provided.

Necessary—The headline bird result is not robust to the alternative learner: FCI emphasizes wing shape/pattern, whereas GRaSP-FCI emphasizes crown color/size and assigns low stability to the former features. This is a substantive reversal rather than reassuring agreement and needs investigation before domain conclusions are drawn.

Necessary—The simulation is only one run of one hand-engineered data-generating process, without repeated recovery metrics or variation in sample size, confounding, density, annotation error, or tuning. The appendix also reports nonzero logistic coefficients for circle and triangle despite asserting that the output depends only on horizontal and vertical bars; if thresholded predictions are invariant to those coefficients, that ground-truth property should be demonstrated explicitly.

Necessary—Observed annotations are treated as if they were causally upstream properties generating pixels, although in both applications the recorded labels are measurements extracted from the same images or reports. A measurement/intervention model is needed to connect interventions on the conceptual feature to changes in an image and hence to the classifier; otherwise the causal estimand is ambiguous.

Optional—The qualitative comparison with a few selected LIME and SHAP visualizations is not an informative benchmark because those methods answer local pixel-attribution questions while the proposal answers a global concept-level question. Comparative superiority claims should be removed or evaluated through a prespecified quantitative or user-centered study; releasing code, splits, seeds, and complete training/search settings would also improve reproducibility.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important, identifiable need: model-agnostic explanations at the level of human-interpretable features while allowing latent confounding. This should interest both causal-discovery and explainable-AI researchers. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-ejur4crt/call-3b790543644747f79584eefa22286f98/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The counterfactual motivation, distinction between micro- and macro-level explanations, and introduction to PAG endpoint semantics are generally clear and pedagogically useful.

The simulation effectively illustrates how an omitted feature can confound an association with a classifier output, while the bird and X-ray studies demonstrate a feasible end-to-end auditing workflow.

The paper discusses several genuine limitations, including dependence on background knowledge, feature construction, annotation error, and finite-sample causal discovery; the writing is organized and accessible.
weaknesses: Necessary — The empirical ranking examines only edges incident to the prediction. A feature can causally affect the prediction through another observed macro-feature without being adjacent to it, so non-adjacency does not justify statements that other variables are causally irrelevant. The analysis should instead evaluate definite and possible ancestry in the complete PAG, or explicitly narrow its claims to prediction-adjacent relations.

Necessary — The reported stability score pools definite-cause edges (Zi→Ŷ) with ambiguous edges (Zi○→Ŷ). The latter only leave causation possible and can represent pure confounding; frequent bootstrap occurrence is not calibrated confidence that Zi is causal. These edge types must be reported separately, and terms such as “likely cause” should be reserved for conclusions actually entailed by the PAG.

Necessary — Evidence for finite-sample causal recovery is inadequate. There is one hand-designed simulation result without repeated trials, recovery metrics, sample-size curves, or comparisons under varying omitted confounders. The real datasets have no causal ground truth, and clinical or ornithological plausibility does not validate causal correctness. Broader repeated simulations or interventional/counterfactual validation are needed; otherwise the real-data claims should be narrowed to hypothesis generation.

Necessary — The discrete conditional-independence tests are potentially unreliable: the bird analysis conditions on as many as four mostly five-level variables with a nine-level outcome, while the X-ray analysis has only 240 observations. This creates very sparse contingency tables for asymptotic chi-square tests. Bootstrap stability does not repair invalid or low-powered tests. Cell-count diagnostics, suitable sparse-data tests, and sensitivity to alpha and conditioning depth are needed.

Necessary — Robustness is weaker than stated: FCI ranks Wing Shape, Wing Pattern, and Tail Shape highest, whereas GRaSP-FCI ranks Crown Color and Size highest. This materially changes the main bird interpretation. The discrepancy should be analyzed and reflected in the conclusions. Reproducibility also requires resolving the conflicting descriptions of background knowledge (Ŷ merely being a non-ancestor versus being a descendant of the interpretable features) and specifying exact model outputs, splits, seeds, training settings, and TETRAD options.

Optional — The LIME/SHAP comparison contrasts local pixel attribution with a global, annotation-dependent causal analysis and uses selected qualitative examples, so it does not establish superiority. Recast it as an illustration of different explanatory targets or add quantitative macro-feature baselines. The Shapley derivation and several typographical or equation-formatting issues should also be checked.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important problem: post-hoc auditing of black-box models using human-interpretable macro-features rather than pixels. This framing should interest both causal-discovery and explainable-AI researchers.

Using PAGs and FCI appropriately acknowledges latent confounding and, under the stated Markov and faithfulness assumptions, can distinguish definite causal ancestry, definite non-ancestry, and unresolved orientation. The formal setup and synthetic example communicate the central intuition well.

The paper is generally clear and self-contained. It discusses dependence on background knowledge, annotation availability, and measurement error, and it includes GRaSP-FCI as a useful sensitivity analysis. The reviewed manuscript is :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-rq21g6e7/call-f2582dcac7274c84a49233e0502eb057/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
weaknesses: Necessary: The real-data evidence does not establish the claimed causal explanations. Neither application has causal ground truth or macro-feature interventions; clinical or ornithological plausibility cannot validate learned arrows. The authors should add interventional or semi-synthetic validation and replicated simulations with recovery metrics, or narrow these results to hypothesis generation.

Necessary: The X-ray design selects pneumonia cases and controls explicitly labeled “no findings,” so selection depends on the condition and candidate findings and creates structural zeros. Together with only 240 observations and potentially high-order chi-square tests, this undermines FCI’s finite-sample reliability. The multi-category bird analysis has analogous sparse-contingency concerns. Bootstrap edge frequency neither repairs invalid CI tests nor constitutes calibrated causal confidence.

Necessary: Edge stability merges definite edges Zi→Ŷ with ambiguous Zi○→Ŷ, even though the latter permits pure latent confounding. It also considers only adjacency, missing indirect causal ancestors allowed by the paper’s own SCM. Claims that low-scoring or nonadjacent variables are causally irrelevant are therefore unsupported. The analysis should separately report definite, possible, and excluded ancestry using paths in the full PAG.

Necessary: The assumed causal status of the annotations is insufficiently justified. CUB attributes and text-mined radiology findings are measurements derived from images or reports, whereas the SCM treats them as manipulable causes of pixels. An explicit latent-attribute and measurement model is needed; otherwise intervening on a recorded label would not change the black-box prediction.

Necessary: It is unclear whether causal discovery uses an audit sample held out from model training; the bootstrap description appears to use all images. Important reproducibility details are also missing, including real-model training settings, seeds, exact discovery options, and edge-type frequencies. The Shapley example requires clarification because f′ is undefined and the supposedly omitted Z3 remains in the resulting attribution.

Optional: The comparison uses a few selected local LIME/SHAP visualizations against a global semantic graph, so it cannot support comparative-superiority claims. A concept-level or global baseline and an aggregate or user-centered evaluation would be more appropriate.

strengths: The paper identifies a relevant, under-addressed setting: explaining black-box predictors globally using human-interpretable macro-features when causally relevant features may be omitted.

The reduction to learning a PAG over annotations and model outputs is intuitive. Under appropriate Markov, faithfulness, no-selection, and background-knowledge assumptions, FCI appropriately avoids assuming causal sufficiency.
The SCM formulation, PAG edge interpretations, Shapley example, and geometric-shape simulation make the distinction between causation, association, and latent confounding accessible.
The bird and X-ray studies illustrate the proposed workflow on realistic annotated-image tasks. Including GRaSP-FCI as a sensitivity analysis usefully reveals method dependence.
The manuscript is generally clear, well organized, and candid about dependence on user-selected features, domain knowledge, annotation quality, and the limited informativeness of PAGs.
weaknesses: Necessary — The real-data causal conclusions are not adequately supported. Neither application has interventions or known causal ground truth, and the identifying assumptions are asserted rather than defended. Most seriously, the X-ray sample contrasts pneumonia cases with controls selected specifically to have “no findings,” so inclusion depends on the diagnosis/report features being analyzed. Treating selection bias as irrelevant is unjustified, and clinically plausible associations cannot validate that atelectasis, infiltration, or effusion causes the model output. These results should be presented as exploratory unless selection is modeled or controlled interventions are added.

Necessary — The principal summary conflates Zi→Yhat, which establishes definite ancestry under the assumptions, with Zi○→Yhat, which remains compatible with pure latent confounding. A high combined bootstrap frequency therefore is not “confidence in causal status” and does not demonstrate the promised causal-versus-confounded distinction. Moreover, analyzing only adjacency to Yhat misses indirect causes such as Zi→Zj→Yhat. Endpoint types should be reported separately and definite/possible ancestral paths analyzed, or the claims should be narrowed to adjacent candidate causes.

Necessary — Validation is too limited for the broad utility claims. The simulation contains one favorable hand-designed DGP, one large sample, and one learned graph, without Monte Carlo recovery metrics, baselines, or stress tests for sample size, weak effects, graph density, deterministic outputs, and annotation error. The bird conclusions are also highly method-sensitive: FCI’s leading Wing Shape, Wing Pattern, and Tail Shape variables fall near the bottom under GRaSP-FCI, whose leaders are Crown Color and Size. Characterizing these findings as broadly similar is misleading.

Necessary — The finite-sample reliability of the discovery analyses is unclear. Chi-square conditional-independence tests involving 26 multi-category bird attributes, a nine-class output, and conditioning sets as large as four can yield extremely sparse contingency tables; the X-ray graph uses only 240 selected observations. The paper provides no cell-count diagnostics, alpha sensitivity, error calibration, stability-selection threshold, or uncertainty intervals. Bootstrap edge frequencies alone neither control false discoveries nor warrant a confidence interpretation.

Necessary — Reproducibility and specification are incomplete: exact X-ray sample/patient identifiers and patient-level splitting, which observations enter structure learning, random seeds, software versions, complete FCI settings, and executable code are absent. The main text says only that Yhat cannot cause Z, whereas Appendix B says Yhat “must be a descendant” of the interpretable features; the implemented constraint must be clarified. The Shapley section also leaves f′ undefined and does not specify the omitted-Z3 estimand clearly enough to audit the algebra.

Optional — The selected default-setting LIME and SHAP visualizations are an interface illustration, not convincing comparative evidence. A stronger comparison would aggregate local attributions, include applicable black-box concept-level baselines, predefine example selection, and use domain-expert or intervention-based evaluation. Minor proofreading and clearer figure labels would also help.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important problem: explaining black-box predictions using human-interpretable macro-level features while allowing latent confounding. This is relevant to both causal-discovery and explainable-AI audiences. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-yknknz80/call-bd1c29564e524e9b8c08ce427523b158/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Using PAGs and the known non-ancestry of image features with respect to the prediction is a sensible qualitative framework under the stated Markov, faithfulness, sampling, and conditional-independence assumptions. The paper explains the relevant causal-graph concepts accessibly.

The distinction between population-level causal explanation and local pixel attribution is useful and clearly motivated. The combination of a simulation, two applications, bootstrapping, and a GRaSP-FCI sensitivity analysis gives readers a concrete view of the proposed workflow.
The writing is generally organized and self-contained, and the limitations concerning background knowledge, annotation availability, and measurement error are discussed candidly.
weaknesses: Necessary: The principal causal interpretation is overstated. Figure 8 pools Zi→Yhat with Zi◦→Yhat, although the latter is also compatible with pure latent confounding. Its bootstrap frequency is therefore stability of an ambiguous adjacency, not confidence that Zi is causal. The real-data discussion nevertheless calls these features “likely causes.” The two edge types must be reported separately and validated against interventions or known ground truth, or the claims must be narrowed to exploratory possible determinants.

Necessary: The finite-sample validity of the conditional-independence tests is not established. The bird analysis combines 26 mostly multi-category variables and a nine-category outcome, conditions on as many as four variables, and uses only 3,538 observations; the X-ray analysis has only 240 observations. This can produce extremely sparse contingency tables for chi-square tests. The depth restriction also removes FCI's general consistency guarantee. Bootstrap frequencies are uncalibrated and do not themselves control false discoveries. Cell-count diagnostics, matched simulations, and sensitivity to test choice, alpha, and conditioning depth are needed.

Necessary: The simulation does not establish its asserted causal ground truth. The reported logistic coefficients for circle and triangle are nonzero (0.0904 and 0.0741), and the shared HydraNet representation permits changes in those shapes to alter the horizontal/vertical-head predictions. Consequently, inspecting coefficients does not prove that only H and V cause the final output. Structural zeros or direct intervention tests are needed, followed by repeated simulations reporting graph-recovery error rather than one favorable run.

Necessary: Ranking only edges adjacent to Yhat misses indirect causes such as Zi→Zj→Yhat, even though causal relations among the Z variables are explicitly allowed. Conversely, absence of adjacency does not imply lack of an interventionist effect. The analysis should examine definite and possible ancestral paths or explicitly narrow its target to adjacency rather than general causal relevance.

Necessary: The real-data designs do not independently validate causal recovery. The X-ray cohort contrasts pneumonia cases with “no findings” controls selected using related report-derived labels, making selection and label construction central to the observed associations; the structure-learning sample, separation from model training, and patient-level independence are unclear. In the bird experiment, arbitrary category consolidation and outcome balancing can materially affect independences, while GRaSP-FCI changes the leading features from wing shape/pattern to crown color/size. These issues require clearer target populations, independent explanation data, selection/clustering analysis, justified preprocessing, and stronger robustness checks.

Necessary: Reproducibility is insufficient for the empirical claims. Real-model training hyperparameters, random seeds, exact splits, the data supplied to FCI, detailed edge counts separated by endpoint type, and executable code are not provided. These details are needed to recreate and audit the reported graphs.

Optional: The LIME/SHAP comparison uses selected local visualizations and evaluates a different explanatory task from the proposed global concept-level analysis. It should either be presented only as an illustration or replaced by comparisons with relevant global or concept-level methods and, ideally, domain-expert evaluation. Several plots also have labels too small for easy reading.

strengths: The manuscript motivates a useful distinction between pixel-level attribution and type-level causal explanations using human-interpretable macro-features; this is relevant to researchers in causal discovery, explainable AI, and model auditing. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-076t8930/call-ed22952608974f6691c0fe7d177c8434/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The query-only setup is practically meaningful, and using PAG learning rather than causally sufficient DAG learning is a principled way to allow latent confounding among the selected features.

The causal assumptions and the meanings of directed, bidirected, and partially oriented PAG edges are presented accessibly. The synthetic example usefully illustrates how an omitted feature can confound an association with the model output.

The two application domains, bootstrap analyses, and GRaSP-FCI sensitivity check demonstrate how the proposed workflow could be used in practice without requiring a new causal-discovery algorithm or state-of-the-art predictive performance.

The paper is generally clear and candid about several limitations, including dependence on background knowledge, finite-sample conditional-independence errors, feature selection, deterministic relations, and annotation measurement error.
weaknesses: Necessary: The central empirical claim that the approach reliably distinguishes causal features from confounded ones is supported by only one favorable synthetic construction and one learned graph, without repeated trials, recovery metrics, uncertainty, or variation in sample size, confounding, graph density, annotation noise, and faithfulness violations. The real-data studies have no causal ground truth or interventions; clinical or ornithological plausibility does not validate the inferred directions. Substantially broader controlled validation is needed, or the claims must be narrowed to a proof-of-concept illustration.

Necessary: Figure 8 pools definite-cause edges (Zi→Yhat) with ambiguous edges (Zi○→Yhat). The latter remain compatible with pure latent confounding, so their bootstrap frequency is not a calibrated confidence that Zi is causal. This aggregation discards the distinction on which the paper's contribution rests, yet the resulting ranking is interpreted as identifying likely causes. Frequencies for every endpoint type should be reported separately, with partially oriented edges described as unresolved rather than causal evidence.

Necessary: The validity of the real-data PAGs is insufficiently established. The X-ray analysis has only 240 observations for higher-order categorical chi-square tests, making sparse contingency cells and low power likely. The bird analysis truncates conditioning sets at size four, which generally removes the stated FCI recovery guarantee. Moreover, selecting pneumonia cases against exclusively “no findings” controls conditions on radiological status and may introduce selection effects, despite the manuscript declaring selection bias irrelevant. Cell-count diagnostics, robustness to tests and tuning parameters, and an explicit treatment of sampling/selection are required.

Necessary: The assumed causal role Z→X is not justified for the observed variables. Bird annotations and text-mined radiology labels are measurements derived from images or reports, not necessarily the manipulable physical properties that generate pixels. Treating noisy, coarsened labels as the causal macro-variables can reverse the relevant measurement relationship and invalidate intervention-based interpretations. The paper needs a measurement model or domain-supported argument linking annotations to latent physical features, and should otherwise limit conclusions to relations among observed proxies.

Necessary: Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript does not provide its analysis code, seeds, detailed real-model training settings, exact bootstrap edge counts, contingency diagnostics, or a clear statement that structure learning used predictions on a held-out query set. These details are important because graph orientations can be sensitive to sampling, preprocessing, and conditional-independence-test settings.

Optional: The qualitative LIME/SHAP comparison uses selected images and default settings while contrasting local pixel explanations with a global method supplied with external semantic annotations; Deep SHAP also assumes more model access than the stated query-only setting. This section should be framed as illustrative or replaced with a controlled comparison to query-only, concept-level, and association-based alternatives.

strengths: The paper identifies a useful problem for causal-inference and XAI researchers: global, type-level explanations in human-interpretable macro-features when only black-box predictions are observable. This is meaningfully different from pixel-level attribution. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-yivc5p2f/call-e4d38f7e65774887a6fff52f74c6e88d/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The SCM, latent-projection, PAG, and FCI formulation is coherent under the stated acyclicity, Markov, faithfulness, and background-knowledge assumptions. The distinction among definite causes, possible causes, and latent-confounded associations is potentially valuable.

The synthetic example clearly illustrates how an omitted macro-feature can confound an observed feature–prediction association. The bird and X-ray studies demonstrate an end-to-end workflow, while GRaSP-FCI provides a useful sensitivity check.

The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, and it explicitly discusses important limitations involving background knowledge, feature construction, measurement error, and finite-sample causal discovery.
weaknesses: Necessary clarification: the real-data results do not validate causal effects because neither study provides interventional evidence or causal ground truth. Figure 8 also pools directed edges with circle-to-arrow edges, although the latter permit pure latent confounding, and bootstrap edge frequency is not calibrated causal confidence. Claims such as “likely causes” should therefore be narrowed to assumption-conditional candidate causes, with the edge types reported separately.

The X-ray design particularly strains the assumptions: the 120 controls are selected to have “no findings,” so the seven report-derived attributes are absent among controls by construction. This feature-dependent selection creates severe support problems and conflicts with the assertion that selection bias is irrelevant. With only 240 observations, chi-square conditional-independence tests can also have very sparse strata; analogous diagnostics are missing for the 26 multi-category bird attributes.

Necessary correction: the main text says the only background constraint is that the prediction cannot cause a feature, whereas Appendix B says the prediction “must be a descendant” of the interpretable features; these are not equivalent. Exact TETRAD constraints, software version, preprocessing code, seeds, and prediction-generation protocol are needed to determine whether orientations were learned or partly imposed.

The Shapley motivation contains technical ambiguities: the displayed general weight omits a factorial, the value function is not defined precisely, and Appendix A.2 leaves the supposedly omitted variable Z3 inside the calculated attribution. This example should be corrected or removed.

Optional strengthening: one favorable, large-sample synthetic run is insufficient to characterize reliability. Repeated simulations across sample sizes, graph densities, latent structures, measurement error, and assumption violations—with adjacency and orientation metrics—would make the scope much clearer.

The qualitative LIME/SHAP comparison uses selected examples and compares local pixel explanations with a global concept-level procedure, so it does not establish superiority. Moreover, FCI and GRaSP-FCI yield substantially different leading bird features. Quantitative concept-level baselines and a more direct discussion of this instability would improve the empirical case.

Please evaluate the paper critically using the journal's acceptance criteria and give an overall recommendation according to the scale below.

First assess whether the claims are supported by accurate and convincing evidence. Material gaps may require additional evidence or narrower claims. Then assess whether some members of the intended research audience could learn something of interest and whether the writing communicates those findings clearly enough to understand and use them.

Do not impose a conference-style significance threshold or require a new method or state-of-the-art performance as a condition of acceptance. Distinguish the basic publication criteria from exceptional-impact certifications. Explain necessary changes separately from optional improvements, using the supplied manuscript without assuming a rebuttal or revisions that are not present.

Assign Overall Assessment (OA) using only: 1, 2, 3, or 4.
These numbers are an experimental ordinal encoding of TMLR's textual reviewer recommendations, not an official TMLR numerical score. They do not define equal distances between recommendations.

Rating scale:
1 = reject
The current work fails a required acceptance criterion in a substantive way.

2 = leaning reject
Important concerns about a required criterion remain unresolved, although the work has a plausible path toward satisfying it.

3 = leaning accept
The evidence generally supports both acceptance criteria, with limited reservations that should be stated precisely.

4 = accept
The claims are adequately supported, the findings have an identifiable interested audience, and the paper communicates them clearly enough for that audience.

Output Format

strengths: The manuscript addresses a useful problem for causal-discovery and explainable-AI researchers: explaining black-box outputs through human-interpretable macro-features while allowing latent confounding. The PAG/FCI framing is an actionable idea requiring only annotated inputs and queried predictions.

The exposition clearly distinguishes association from interventionist explanation, explains PAG endpoint semantics, and states important assumptions such as faithfulness, causal background knowledge, feature manipulability, and annotation quality.

The synthetic example provides an intuitive illustration of how an omitted feature can confound an observed feature-output association. The two application domains and GRaSP-FCI sensitivity analysis broaden the discussion beyond that toy setting.
The paper is generally readable and well organized, with helpful diagrams and substantial discussion of practical limitations.
weaknesses: Necessary: The proposed feature ranking examines only edges adjacent to the prediction. This does not identify all causal determinants under the paper's own model, which permits relations among macro-features. For example, Zi→Zj→Yhat makes Zi causally relevant despite no Zi-Yhat edge. The analysis must examine definite and possible ancestral paths, or explicitly narrow its claims to adjacent/proximal relations and stop treating nonadjacent features as causally irrelevant.

Necessary: The evidence is insufficient for the broad claim that the method reliably separates causal from confounded features. There is only one favorable, low-dimensional synthetic instance, with no repeated trials, recovery metrics, sample-size or effect-strength sweeps, graph variations, or comparisons against associational and causally insufficient baselines. The real-data results lack causal ground truth or intervention-based validation, so clinical or ornithological plausibility cannot validate the inferred directions. Substantially broader controlled evaluation is needed, or the claims should be narrowed to exploratory hypothesis generation.

Necessary: The finite-sample validity of the conditional-independence tests is not established. The bird analysis applies chi-square tests to many multi-category variables with conditioning sets up to size four, while the X-ray analysis has only 240 observations; the resulting contingency tables can be extremely sparse. Truncating FCI's conditioning depth also removes its general consistency guarantee unless suitable graph-degree conditions hold. Sparse-cell diagnostics, calibration experiments, and sensitivity to alpha and depth are needed.

Necessary: Bootstrap edge frequency is called confidence in causal status, but it is neither a calibrated probability nor an error-controlled stability measure. Moreover, combining Zi→Yhat with Zi○→Yhat conflates definite ancestry with ambiguity that includes pure confounding. These edge types and path-level conclusions should be reported separately with uncertainty. This matters especially because GRaSP-FCI changes the leading bird features from Wing Shape/Wing Pattern/Tail Shape to Crown Color/Size and related attributes.

Necessary: The X-ray design selects pneumonia cases against only 'No Finding' controls, making the control finding indicators zero by construction and risking selection-induced or dataset-artifact associations. Patient-level independence, train/test overlap, and whether causal discovery used an audit set independent of classifier training are also unclear. The causal analysis should be repeated under a defensible sampling design with an independent query set.

Necessary: The selected LIME/SHAP images compare local pixel attribution with global macro-feature causal discovery—different inputs and estimands—and therefore do not substantiate comparative superiority. strengths: The complete manuscript, including its figures and appendices, is generally well organized and readable :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-94lgnji3/call-199f13bb6e8c44a5a2a036a22be9dc8c/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}. It provides enough background on PAGs and FCI for an XAI audience to follow the proposal.
The motivation is useful: macro-level concepts can be more actionable than pixels, and omitted concepts can confound associations between recorded concepts and model outputs.

Subject to causal Markov, faithfulness, measurement, and intervention assumptions, using a PAG with the constraint that predictions cannot cause pre-existing image properties is a principled way to represent uncertainty from latent confounding.
The synthetic data-generating process is transparent, and the paper illustrates the workflow on two applications. Including GRaSP-FCI as a sensitivity analysis is also valuable.

The work has an identifiable audience spanning causal discovery, explainable AI, and algorithm auditing; a new causal-discovery algorithm or state-of-the-art predictive performance is not needed for that audience to find the question interesting.
weaknesses: Necessary — The central empirical claim is not convincingly established. The only ground-truth experiment is one favorable, hand-designed simulation with 20,000 observations, strong effects, and no repeated runs, recovery metrics, sample-size study, noise study, or comparison against methods that ignore confounding. The two real-data studies have no causal ground truth or interventions; clinical or intuitive plausibility cannot validate learned directions. The claims should be narrowed to hypothesis generation, or supported by substantially broader simulations and interventional or otherwise ground-truthed validation.

Necessary — Finite-sample reliability is especially doubtful. The X-ray analysis has only 240 observations but performs high-order chi-square conditional-independence tests over seven binary findings and the prediction. The bird analysis combines 26 multi-category variables and caps conditioning sets at four, which removes the usual FCI consistency guarantee unless an additional structural condition is justified. Sparse-cell diagnostics, power analyses, suitable tests, and sensitivity to alpha, conditioning depth, sample size, and effect strength are absent.

Necessary — Bootstrap edge frequency is not calibrated causal confidence and does not by itself control false discoveries. Moreover, the reported score merges Zi→Ŷ, which supports definite ancestry under the assumptions, with Zi○→Ŷ, which leaves ancestry versus confounding unresolved. Calling both 'likely causes,' and treating absent edges as evidence of causal irrelevance, materially overstates what the PAGs and low-powered tests establish. Endpoint types and uncertainty should be reported separately and interpreted conservatively.

Necessary — The causal semantics of the observed concepts are not established. Bird attributes and radiology findings are annotations or proxies derived from images and reports, rather than demonstrated manipulable variables that cause pixels as assumed by the SCM. Measurement error is only mentioned, not incorporated. The X-ray case/control construction—particularly selecting controls with 'no findings'—also creates an unmodeled selection mechanism. The paper must justify well-defined interventions, measurement assumptions, and selection assumptions before presenting these results as causal explanations.

Necessary — The robustness evidence is unfavorable but understated: FCI ranks Wing Shape and Wing Pattern highest in the bird study, whereas GRaSP-FCI ranks Crown Color and Size highest and gives generally lower stability. This disagreement concerns the main substantive conclusion, so it should be analyzed as instability rather than summarized as broadly similar behavior.

Necessary — The Shapley example is not operationally clear. After Z3 is declared omitted, its value still appears in the purportedly incorrect attribution, and the comparison simultaneously changes the player set and adjustment information. The manuscript does not show what quantity could actually be estimated from the observed variables in its black-box setting. A precise estimand and derivation are needed for this example to support the criticism of existing methods.

Necessary — Reproducibility and data-use details are insufficient: there is no implementation repository or random seeds, exact software versions and several training choices are missing, and it is unclear whether causal discovery uses predictions on independent held-out images or on observations used to train the networks. An independent query set is important for the i.i.d. structure-learning interpretation.

Necessary if retained — The LIME/SHAP comparison uses selected qualitative examples and default settings, while those methods provide local pixel-level explanations and the proposal provides population-level concept graphs. This does not support comparative superiority. The claim should be removed or evaluated against appropriate global and concept-level baselines with a quantitative or user-centered protocol.

Optional — A concise assumption-to-conclusion table would improve usability, and several typographical or reporting issues should be corrected, including 'Dependance,' 'verticies,' 'exhuastively,' the ambiguous momentum value 0.09, and the statement that excluded bird labels 'did fit' the retained groups. Overall, the audience and exposition criterion is met, but the evidence criterion remains unresolved, yielding a leaning-reject assessment.

strengths: The manuscript identifies an important distinction between pixel-level attribution and explanations using human-interpretable macro-features, especially when omitted concepts induce latent confounding. This should interest researchers in causal discovery, XAI, and algorithm auditing. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-qew_3_kw/call-206e1a2ccf2648578f83c1d159b450b7/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Using a PAG-learning method with the defensible constraint that predictions cannot cause pre-existing image features is conceptually appropriate for a query-only black-box setting with possible latent confounders.
The counterfactual motivation, edge-semantics table, diagrams, Shapley example, and geometric-shape experiment communicate the association-versus-causation issue clearly.

The bird and chest-X-ray applications establish feasibility on multiclass and binary tasks. Including GRaSP-FCI as a sensitivity analysis is useful, and the generally clear writing makes the proposal accessible.
weaknesses: Necessary: The central causal-discrimination claim needs substantially stronger validation. The paper reports one synthetic configuration and one learned graph, without repeated trials, recovery metrics, sample-size/effect-size studies, missing-feature sweeps, or relevant macro-feature baselines. The claimed ground truth also needs clarification: the appendix reports nonzero circle and triangle logistic coefficients but does not specify whether probabilities or hard labels enter and leave the classifier, nor directly verify invariance under interventions on these shapes.

Necessary: The real-data results provide plausibility checks, not evidence that the identified features cause model outputs. No interventions or known causal ground truth are available. The X-ray study is particularly problematic: it has only 240 images, contrasts pneumonia cases with controls explicitly selected for “No Finding,” and derives explanatory labels from the same reports. This restricts support and creates outcome/finding-dependent selection despite the paper treating selection bias as irrelevant; repeated-patient dependence and patient-disjoint splitting are also unaddressed.

Necessary: The conditional-independence testing regime is not convincingly valid. The bird analysis combines 26 multi-category variables and a nine-category prediction with only 3,538 observations, making chi-square tables conditioned on up to four variables extremely sparse; the 240-image X-ray analysis is still less supported. Limiting FCI conditioning depth also removes the direct applicability of its stated consistency guarantee. Cell-count diagnostics, suitable sparse-data tests, depth/alpha sensitivity, and calibrated uncertainty are needed. Raw bootstrap selection frequencies neither control false-discovery rate nor constitute causal confidence.

Necessary: The reported statistic does not justify several causal conclusions. Pooling directed edges with circle-arrow edges conflates definite ancestry with an orientation that remains compatible with pure latent confounding. Considering only adjacency to the prediction also misses indirect causal paths, even though the model explicitly permits causal relations among macro-features. Low stability can represent absence, bidirected confounding, or orientation instability. Full edge-type and possible/definite-ancestry frequencies should be reported, and “likely cause,” “non-causal,” and “important determinant” claims narrowed accordingly.

Necessary: Reproducibility is insufficient for assessing the empirical evidence. Exact real-model training and inference procedures, splits, seeds, whether structure learning uses in-sample predictions, complete FCI/GRaSP settings, and executable code are missing. The manuscript also inconsistently describes its background knowledge as merely forbidding prediction-to-feature causation versus requiring the prediction to be a descendant of the interpretable features.

Necessary for the comparative claims: The LIME/SHAP evaluation uses a few selected images and compares local pixel attributions with a global macro-level structure-learning output. This task mismatch cannot establish comparative superiority or the claimed confounding advantage. A systematic, task-matched evaluation is needed, or these panels should be framed only as motivation.

Optional: Interventional image edits, causal-effect magnitude estimates, and evaluation by domain experts would make the resulting graphs more actionable. These are not required if the paper instead narrows itself to an exploratory structure-learning framework. As written, however, the identifiable audience and clear exposition satisfy the audience criterion, while the unresolved evidential and semantic issues prevent the causal claims from satisfying TMLR’s support criterion.

strengths: The paper identifies a useful gap between pixel-level attribution and explanations expressed in human-interpretable, potentially manipulable macro-features. Its distinction between association and interventionist difference-making is well motivated and relevant to causal-discovery and explainable-AI audiences.

Using PAG learning rather than assuming causal sufficiency is conceptually appropriate. The manuscript clearly explains the relevant FCI edge semantics, latent-confounding motivation, background knowledge, faithfulness requirement, and type-level nature of the proposed explanations.

The synthetic example makes the omitted-feature problem concrete, while the bird and radiograph studies illustrate an end-to-end workflow. Including GRaSP-FCI as a sensitivity analysis is helpful and exposes instability in the bird rankings rather than concealing it.

The manuscript is generally clear, well organized, and visually readable. It candidly discusses dependence on expert annotations, background knowledge, sample size, identifiability, and measurement error. The framing itself offers an identifiable audience something useful even though the underlying discovery algorithms are established methods.
weaknesses: Necessary: The real-data conclusions are stronger than the evidence permits. Figure 8 combines frequencies of directed Zi -> Yhat edges with Zi o-> Yhat edges, although the latter remain compatible with pure latent confounding. Thus statements that the highly ranked attributes are "likely causes" do not follow from the plotted statistic alone. Report the endpoint types separately and describe these results as exploratory possible-cause hypotheses unless independent interventional validation is added.

Necessary: Finite-sample reliability is insufficiently established. The bird analysis applies chi-square conditional-independence tests to 26 multi-category variables with conditioning sets up to size four, while the radiograph analysis has only 240 observations. Sparse contingency tables can invalidate these tests, and bootstrap selection frequency is not calibrated causal confidence. Cell-count diagnostics, repeated simulations across sample sizes, and sensitivity to alpha, conditioning depth, and alternative discrete tests are needed. The pneumonia-versus-"no findings" case-control construction, possible repeated patients, and report-derived features also require explicit treatment as potential selection and dependence mechanisms.

Necessary: The simulation does not fully establish its asserted causal ground truth. The learned HydraNet can allow changes in circles or triangles to alter its horizontal/vertical predictions, and the downstream logistic model has nonzero circle and triangle coefficients. The paper should specify whether FCI receives a hard label or score and verify invariance through paired interventions that change one shape while holding the others and noise fixed. Repeated recovery metrics would be more convincing than one displayed PAG.

Necessary: Appendix A's Shapley counterexample appears mathematically inconsistent as written. In A.2, Z3 is said to be unmeasured but remains in expressions after integration over only Z1 and Z2; moreover, several A.1 expectations use observational marginals even though interventions on Z2 or Z3 should change their descendant Z1. The estimand and post-intervention distributions must be defined and the derivation corrected, or this supporting claim should be removed.

Necessary: Reproducibility details are incomplete, including exact real-model training settings, random seeds, construction of graph-learning samples, whether training-set predictions are queried, patient-disjoint splitting, and full TETRAD/background-knowledge configuration. The statement in Appendix B that Yhat "must be a descendant" of the interpretable features should also be reconciled with the weaker non-ancestor restriction stated in the main text.

Optional: The selected-image LIME/SHAP comparison is qualitative and compares local pixel attribution with a global macro-feature graph, so it does not substantiate the claimed advantage regarding confounding. A controlled comparison with causal or concept-level baselines, plus quantitative or user-centered evaluation, would strengthen the paper but is not essential if this section is explicitly presented only as illustration.

strengths: The manuscript addresses a clearly scoped and practically relevant problem: producing global, macro-level explanations of black-box predictions while allowing latent confounding. This should interest researchers in causal discovery, explainable AI, and algorithm auditing. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-k0egp16p/call-c9374fe801ab45b7851ffe5e59e3096d/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Using PAGs rather than causally sufficient DAG models is conceptually appropriate for user-selected feature sets that may omit relevant variables. The paper explains the relevant FCI edge semantics and assumptions accessibly.

The analytical example and geometric-shape simulation effectively illustrate how an omitted feature can confound a macro-feature/output association and how causal discovery could distinguish this from a causal relation.

The presentation is generally clear and self-contained, with useful diagrams and candid discussion of faithfulness, limited informativeness, annotation requirements, measurement error, and the role of domain knowledge.
The bird and X-ray studies demonstrate feasibility, while the GRaSP-FCI analysis provides at least one meaningful robustness check rather than presenting a single algorithmic output.
weaknesses: Necessary: The real-data experiments do not validate the central causal interpretations. There are no interventions, known causal ground truth, or independent expert validation; clinical relevance and intuitive salience establish plausibility, not that the classifier actually uses those attributes. Moreover, GRaSP-FCI changes the leading bird features from Wing Shape/Wing Pattern/Tail Shape to Crown Color/Size, contradicting the claimed robustness of the substantive conclusion. These results should be presented as hypothesis generation unless stronger validation is added.

Necessary: The proposed edge-stability statistic is not calibrated evidence that a feature is causal. It pools definite ancestry (Zi→Ŷ) with the ambiguous Zi○→Ŷ case, which explicitly also permits pure latent confounding. The imposed non-ancestry of Ŷ already constrains the outcome endpoint, and bootstrap selection frequency is not a posterior probability or confidence measure. Conversely, absence of adjacency to Ŷ does not imply causal irrelevance because a feature may affect Ŷ through another observed feature. Claims that low-ranked attributes are not causal therefore exceed what the reported PAG summaries establish.

Necessary: The conditional-independence analysis lacks finite-sample justification. The bird experiment combines a nine-level outcome with multi-category attributes and conditioning sets of up to four variables, creating very sparse contingency tables even with 3,538 observations; the X-ray experiment has only 240 observations and rare findings. No expected-cell diagnostics, power analysis, alternative tests, or error calibration is provided. Restricting FCI's conditioning-set size to four also removes its general consistency guarantee unless an appropriate graph-degree assumption is established. Bootstrap frequencies and arbitrarily chosen alpha levels do not repair biased or underpowered chi-square tests.

Necessary: The X-ray sampling design is especially problematic. Controls are selected using a “no findings” report while the explanatory variables are themselves report-mined findings, inducing severe selection and near-deterministic absence of those variables among controls. This conflicts with the paper's dismissal of selection bias and can create the reported structure independently of classifier reliance. Patient-level splitting is not stated despite multiple images per patient, and it is unclear whether causal discovery uses an independent audit set or images used to train the classifier.

Necessary: The single simulation is illustrative rather than convincing validation. It reports one recovered graph without repeated graph-recovery metrics, false-positive rates, variation over sample size/effect strength, or comparisons under realistic sparsity. Because the black box contains a learned feature detector and logistic coefficients for Circle and Triangle are nonzero, the asserted causal ground truth also needs direct intervention verification or a construction that enforces exact invariance.

Necessary: Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript does not provide code, software versions, random seeds, real-model training settings, exact bootstrap construction, the dataset split used for structure learning, or complete FCI configuration. The appendix's statement that Ŷ “must be a descendant” of the features is also stronger than the main text's non-ancestor constraint and should be reconciled.

Optional: The LIME/SHAP comparison contrasts local pixel attribution with a global, annotation-dependent causal analysis and uses only selected examples with default settings. It illustrates different output types but does not support comparative superiority; this section should be reframed or supplemented with task-matched concept-level baselines and a quantitative or user-centered evaluation.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important, identifiable problem: post-hoc, type-level explanation using human-interpretable macro-features when model internals are unavailable. Using PAGs rather than causally sufficient DAGs or CPDAGs is conceptually appropriate when the analyst may omit relevant macro-features. The paper gives an accessible account of FCI, latent confounding, and the relevant edge semantics.

The geometric-shape example clearly illustrates the intended failure mode: an omitted feature can confound the association between an observed feature and the prediction. It is pedagogically effective even though broader validation is needed.

The two applications demonstrate that the proposed workflow can be run on annotated image datasets. The paper reports sample sizes, classifier accuracies, bootstrap settings, FCI tuning choices, feature preprocessing, and an alternative GRaSP-FCI analysis.

The exposition is generally clear, and the discussion appropriately acknowledges dependence on background knowledge, the difficulty of obtaining manipulable annotations, measurement error, and the distinction between type-level and instance-level explanations.
weaknesses: Necessary: The principal empirical score pools Zi→Yhat with Zi○→Yhat. The latter explicitly remains compatible with pure latent confounding, so its repeated occurrence is not evidence that Zi is probably causal. Since the arrowhead at Yhat is also partly supplied by the background constraint, descriptions such as “confidence in causal status,” “likely causes,” and “important determinants” are unsupported. Definite and ambiguous orientations should be reported separately and the claims narrowed accordingly.

Necessary: Ranking only edges incident to Yhat does not recover all causal determinants. A feature can causally affect Yhat through another observed feature while being nonadjacent to Yhat in the MAG/PAG. Conversely, low incident-edge stability does not show that a feature is causally irrelevant. The analysis needs whole-PAG definite/possible-ancestor path criteria or must explicitly limit its conclusions to adjacency.

Necessary: The finite-sample reliability of the conditional-independence tests is not established. The bird analysis combines 26 multi-category variables and a nine-category prediction with conditioning sets up to size four, while the X-ray analysis has only 240 observations and permits still larger conditioning sets. The resulting contingency tables are likely extremely sparse, making asymptotic chi-square tests unreliable; truncating FCI at depth four also removes its general consistency guarantee. Bootstrap edge frequency is not calibrated confidence or false-discovery control. Expected-cell diagnostics, suitable tests, sensitivity analyses, and simulations matching these regimes are required.

Necessary: The X-ray sampling design creates a serious unaddressed selection problem. The study contrasts 120 pneumonia images with 120 “No Finding” controls, for whom the seven report-derived findings are absent by construction. Thus inclusion depends on the target diagnosis and report findings, yet the causal analysis treats selection bias as irrelevant. A representative cohort, a selection-aware model, or substantially narrower conclusions are needed.

Necessary: The real-data results have no causal ground truth or intervention-based validation; clinical or ornithological plausibility alone cannot verify causal use by the classifier. Moreover, FCI ranks wing shape and wing pattern highest for birds, whereas GRaSP-FCI ranks crown color and size highest. The single simulation run provides no recovery metrics, repetitions, or variation over graph density, effect strength, and missingness. The claimed simulation ground truth should also be verified interventionally because all four head predictions enter the logistic model and the HydraNet representation is shared.

Necessary: The Shapley counterexample is insufficiently defined and appears inconsistent with the stated SCM. If f'_S denotes an interventional value, several displayed terms marginalize Z1 observationally even when interventions on its causes Z2 or Z3 should change its distribution; the omitted-feature calculation also retains Z3 as a fixed quantity. The value function and truncated-factorization calculations need correction or a formal justification.

Necessary: Reproducibility details are incomplete, including which train/validation/test observations enter causal discovery, whether Yhat is a hard label or probability, patient-level splitting for X-rays, real-model optimization and augmentation settings, bootstrap sample construction, random seeds, and exact sample identifiers or code.

Optional: The qualitative comparison with selected LIME and SHAP examples does not establish superiority because those methods answer a different, local pixel-level question and the example-selection protocol is unspecified. This section should be framed as illustration or supplemented with concept-level/global baselines and a user-utility evaluation.

strengths: The paper clearly motivates why causal, macro-level explanations can be more actionable than pixel-level associations and identifies an audience spanning causal discovery and explainable AI.

Using PAGs and FCI is conceptually appropriate when explanatory features may be causally related and relevant variables may be unobserved. The exposition of PAG edge semantics and assumptions is accessible.
The synthetic example provides a useful illustration in which FCI distinguishes a causal feature from one associated with the prediction through an omitted common cause.
The bird and X-ray studies demonstrate how the proposed workflow could be applied, and the GRaSP-FCI sensitivity analysis is valuable even though it exposes instability.
The manuscript is generally clear, pedagogical, and candid about several limitations, including dependence on domain-selected features, faithfulness, finite-sample errors, and annotation noise.
weaknesses: Necessary: The real-data experiments do not validate the claimed causal explanations. Clinical or ornithological plausibility establishes association with the task, not that changing a feature would change the trained model. The results should be presented as exploratory causal hypotheses unless supported by controlled macro-feature interventions, paired edits, or other ground-truth evidence.

Necessary: Figure 8 combines Zi->Yhat and Zi o->Yhat frequencies and interprets the result as confidence in causal status. A circle endpoint also permits a purely confounded, noncausal explanation, so this aggregation removes the distinction central to the paper. Frequencies for directed, partially directed, bidirected, and absent edges should be reported separately, and only invariant tails should support definite-cause language.

Necessary: The X-ray design selects pneumonia cases against controls explicitly labeled No Finding, which makes all seven disease findings absent among controls by construction. This outcome/covariate-dependent selection can manufacture the relevant associations and violates the claim that selection bias is irrelevant. A representative, independently sampled audit cohort is needed, or the population-level causal conclusions must be withdrawn.

Necessary: Finite-sample reliability is not convincing. Chi-square conditional-independence tests with 26 multilevel bird variables and conditioning sets up to four can have extremely sparse cells; the 240-image X-ray analysis permits still larger conditioning sets. Ordinary bootstrap edge frequency neither controls false discoveries nor constitutes calibrated causal confidence. Cell-count diagnostics, suitable tests, repeated simulations across sample sizes and graphs, and graph-recovery metrics are needed.

Necessary: The bird conclusions are materially algorithm-dependent: GRaSP-FCI ranks Crown Color and Size highest rather than Wing Shape and Wing Pattern. This disagreement should constrain the substantive conclusions and be investigated rather than treated as broadly corroborative sensitivity evidence.

Necessary: The causal ontology is insufficiently justified for the applications. Dataset annotations and radiology-report labels are measurements produced from images, whereas the assumed SCM treats the observed macro-features as upstream causes of pixels. The paper needs an explicit latent-attribute/measurement model, validation of annotation quality, or narrower claims about observed labels rather than interventions on physical attributes.

Necessary: It is unclear whether structure learning uses training, validation, test, or all queried images, and whether X-ray splits are patient-disjoint. Real-model training details, random seeds, sampling rules, software versions, and classifier outputs are insufficient for reproduction. An independent audit sample is particularly important here.

Necessary: The Shapley counterexample is under-specified: the coalition value functions are not formally defined, and the purported calculation after omitting Z3 still contains Z3. As written, it is unclear what an analyst without that feature could estimate. The example should be corrected and tied explicitly to the cited causal-Shapley definition.

Necessary: The simulation reports one favorable graph rather than repeated recovery performance, and the fitted logistic model has nonzero coefficients for Circle and Triangle despite the statement that only Horizontal and Vertical are determinants. The paper should clarify whether Yhat is a thresholded label or probability and empirically verify the asserted ground truth.

Optional: A systematic comparison with global concept-level explanation methods would be more informative than selected LIME and SHAP images. This is useful context, but state-of-the-art performance or a new baseline is not required for acceptance.

strengths: The paper identifies a useful and well-motivated target: population-level explanations of black-box behavior in terms of human-interpretable macro-features, while explicitly allowing omitted macro-features to confound observed relationships.

The PAG/FCI framework is explained clearly and has appropriate causal semantics under the stated Markov, faithfulness, background-knowledge, and reliable conditional-independence-testing assumptions. The distinction among definite causes, possible causes, and associations due to latent confounding is especially useful.

The controlled geometric-shape example and the causal-Shapley calculation make the central confounding problem concrete. The bird and X-ray studies further illustrate how the proposed workflow could be used in realistic auditing settings.

The manuscript is unusually accessible across the causal-discovery and explainable-ML communities. It also discusses important limitations involving background knowledge, feature construction, annotation error, and finite-sample graph recovery. This synthesis should interest a recognizable research audience even though it primarily combines existing tools.
weaknesses: Necessary: The real-data results should be characterized more explicitly as exploratory rather than as evidence that particular attributes causally drive the networks. There is no causal ground truth or intervention, and clinical or ornithological plausibility does not validate the learned directions. More seriously, the X-ray controls are selected to have “no findings,” making inclusion depend on the candidate explanatory labels; this introduces selection effects that the stated FCI interpretation treats as irrelevant. The authors should model or avoid this selection, or substantially narrow the causal conclusions.

Necessary: The reliability of the conditional-independence tests is insufficiently established. With 240 X-rays, conditioning on several binary variables produces very sparse contingency tables; with 26 multi-category bird attributes and conditioning sets up to size four, the sparsity can be more severe. Ordinary asymptotic chi-square tests may therefore be badly calibrated, and bootstrapping does not correct systematic test invalidity. Cell-count diagnostics and robust permutation, exact, or regularized alternatives are needed, or the empirical claims should be narrowed.

Necessary: The reported edge-stability score pools definite edges with ambiguous circle-arrow edges and is not a calibrated confidence measure. Moreover, GRaSP-FCI changes the leading bird attributes from Wing Shape/Wing Pattern/Tail Shape to Crown Color/Size. This method dependence materially weakens the specific bird conclusions and should be foregrounded. Separate edge-type frequencies, uncertainty summaries, and repeated simulations across sample sizes and graph regimes would make the evidence substantially more convincing.

Optional: The LIME/SHAP comparison is qualitative, uses selected examples and default settings, and compares local pixel explanations with a global macro-feature objective. It illustrates the difference in goals but does not establish superiority. A clearer scope statement, concept-level baselines where applicable, and fuller reproducibility details—including code, seeds, exact FCI settings, and which data splits supplied graph-learning predictions—would improve the paper.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-sozn8iwj/call-19e89eadbf5e45de94a1f2f13e102b3a/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses an important problem: black-box auditing with human-interpretable macro-features when latent confounding makes ordinary attribution unreliable.

There is an identifiable audience spanning causal discovery, explainable AI, and high-stakes model auditing. The synthesis of latent projections, PAGs, and model explanations is useful even though it primarily combines existing tools; novelty or state-of-the-art performance is not required for TMLR acceptance.

The idealized framework is largely coherent: it states a structural data-generating model, imposes the defensible constraint that model output cannot cause image content, and distinguishes definite, possible, and confounded PAG relations.

The synthetic example illustrates the intended omitted-feature mechanism concretely, while the bird and X-ray studies make the proposed workflow tangible. Providing a GRaSP-FCI sensitivity analysis is also valuable.
The exposition is generally clear and self-contained, with helpful diagrams and candid discussion of faithfulness, background knowledge, annotation noise, and feature construction.
weaknesses: The evidence criterion is not yet met, leading to a leaning-reject assessment. The conceptual proposal is interesting, but the experiments do not convincingly support the manuscript's claims that the reported real-data features are causal determinants or that the procedure reliably separates causes from confounded correlates.

Necessary: The analysis scores only edges directly incident to the prediction node. A feature can causally affect the prediction through another observed macro-feature without being adjacent to the prediction in a MAG/PAG; therefore, absence of an edge does not establish that the feature is causally irrelevant, contrary to several result interpretations and figure captions. The method should analyze definite/possible ancestral paths or narrow its claims to adjacent inducing relations.

Necessary: The finite-sample structure-learning evidence is inadequate. The bird analysis applies chi-square conditional-independence tests to 26 multi-category variables while truncating conditioning sets at four, which forfeits general FCI completeness unless a suitable separator bound is justified. The X-ray analysis has only 240 observations and unrestricted conditioning among binary variables, producing potentially very sparse contingency tables. No cell-count diagnostics, test calibration, repeated simulations at comparable dimensions, or graph-recovery metrics are reported.

Necessary: Bootstrap edge frequency is not itself false-discovery control, a confidence probability, or evidence that an ambiguous relation is causal. Combining Zi→Ŷ with Zi○→Ŷ is particularly problematic because the latter remains compatible with pure latent confounding—the ambiguity the paper aims to resolve. Definite, possible, and bidirected relations should be reported separately, with calibrated uncertainty and appropriately cautious language.

Necessary: The real-data studies have no causal ground truth or intervention-based validation. Clinical and ornithological plausibility, plus selected LIME/SHAP visualizations, establishes neither ancestry nor causal effect. The X-ray design is especially vulnerable because controls are selected for having 'no findings' while the explanatory variables are report-derived findings; this selection and label noise are not incorporated into the assumed graph. Controlled attribute interventions, stronger semisynthetic benchmarks, or substantially narrower claims are needed.

Necessary: The sole synthetic result is one favorable run with 20,000 samples. It lacks repetitions, precision/recall or endpoint-error metrics, variation in sample size and confounding, and comparisons with relevant alternatives. The paper should also verify interventionally that changing C or T cannot alter the hard prediction through the learned HydraNet representation; small nonzero logistic coefficients and high head accuracy alone do not prove this.

Necessary for reproducibility: The manuscript does not adequately specify whether structure learning uses training, validation, test, or pooled predictions; whether splits are patient-disjoint; all real-model training settings; software versions; random seeds; or code. In-sample predictions would also conflict with the fixed-function/i.i.d. abstraction unless carefully justified.

Optional: Clarify the Shapley example's intervention/value function and distinguish a zero local attribution at a selected point from global causal irrelevance. Reporting full learned graphs, causal-effect magnitudes where identifiable, and an expert usefulness evaluation would further strengthen the practical contribution.

strengths: The paper identifies a useful problem: global, macro-level explanations of black-box predictions when omitted concepts can confound observational associations. This should interest causal-discovery and explainable-ML researchers.

PAGs and FCI are, in principle, appropriate tools for representing latent confounding. The exposition of causal graphs, background knowledge, and edge semantics is accessible and largely self-contained.
The geometric-shape example is intuitive, and the inclusion of two application domains plus a GRaSP-FCI sensitivity analysis gives the proposal useful breadth.
The manuscript is organized clearly and candidly discusses limitations involving feature construction, background knowledge, finite-sample discovery, and annotation error.
weaknesses: Necessary: The main causal interpretation is overstated. A Zi circle-to Y-hat edge is compatible with pure latent confounding, yet the experiments pool these edges with definite Zi-to-Y-hat edges and describe the resulting frequency as confidence that Zi is a causal determinant. These edge types must be reported separately, and ambiguous edges must be presented as hypotheses rather than evidence favoring causation.

Necessary: The real-data studies do not establish that the learned edges are correct. There is no interventional ground truth or expert validation. More seriously, the X-ray design selects controls specifically labeled “no findings,” making all seven explanatory findings absent among controls and creating selection and support problems that are outside the stated SCM. The annotations are also image/report-derived proxies, not unambiguously upstream causal variables. These issues require modeling or substantially narrower claims.

Necessary: Statistical validity is insufficiently demonstrated. Chi-square conditional-independence tests can be unreliable for 240 observations and for multi-category bird variables conditioned on up to four other variables. Moreover, limiting FCI's conditioning depth to four removes its stated consistency guarantee. Cell-count diagnostics, sensitivity to alpha and depth, alternative valid tests, and broader repeated simulations with recovery metrics are needed.

Necessary: The simulation does not clearly realize its asserted ground truth. The reported logistic model has nonzero coefficients for circle and triangle despite the claim that predictions depend entirely on horizontal and vertical bars. If thresholded predictions are invariant to those variables, this should be proved empirically; otherwise the reference DAG is incorrect. A single successful graph from one run also provides weak recovery evidence.
Optional: Reproducibility would improve with code, random seeds, complete CNN training details, software versions, numerical edge frequencies, and uncertainty intervals.

Optional: The LIME/SHAP comparison uses selected examples and contrasts local pixel explanations with a deliberately different global concept-level objective. It should be framed as qualitative complementarity or replaced with systematic comparisons, including concept-level baselines or user/domain-expert evaluation.
